chapters.title: Chapter 3: Working Capital Policy and Requirement

lessons.title: Permanent vs Temporary Working Capital and How to Fund Each

children.text: Here is a question that decides how a business should be funded. If your working capital is ₹36 crore at the peak of the season and ₹17 crore in the quietest month, how much working capital does the business actually need?

The answer is both numbers, and they need completely different funding. The ₹17 crore never goes away. The ₹19 crore on top of it appears and disappears every year. Fund them the same way and you either pay too much or take a risk you have not priced.
Watch One Year of a Real Cycle

Himachal Knitwear Ltd makes woollens. Production builds from April, stock peaks before the winter selling season, dealers are supplied through October and November, and collections come in through December and January. Here is its working capital, month by month, in ₹ crore.

body.title: Himachal Knitwear: working capital through the year (₹ crore)

children.text: The flat line at ₹17 crore is the
permanent working capital

. Even in February, the quietest month of the year, the business still has raw wool in stores, part-finished stock on the floor and money owed by dealers. That layer does not convert back to cash unless the business shuts down.

markDefs.definition: The minimum level of working capital the business needs even at its quietest month. It never converts back to cash while the business operates.

children.text: Everything above the line is
temporary working capital
, peaking at ₹19 crore in September. It is genuinely self-liquidating: the stock built in the monsoon becomes dealer invoices in October and cash in January.

markDefs.definition: The additional working capital needed only during peak months, which unwinds into cash when the season ends.

stats.label: Peak requirement
stats.context: September, when finished stock is highest

stats.label: Permanent layer
stats.context: February, the annual trough, and the level that never unwinds

stats.label: Average through the year
stats.context: What a single annual balance sheet figure would suggest

body.text: A 31 March balance sheet would show this company at ₹17 crore, close to its annual low. Read that figure alone and you would badly understate what the business needs in September. This is why seasonal companies must be assessed on monthly data, not the year-end position.

body.title: Split the two layers
body.prompt: Using the chart above, where working capital peaks at ₹36 crore in September and bottoms at ₹17 crore in February, how much temporary working capital does the business need at its peak, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: The permanent layer is the annual minimum of ₹17 crore. The peak is ₹36 crore. The temporary requirement at its highest is the difference, ₹19 crore, and it unwinds completely by February.

children.text: Why the Split Decides the Funding

columns.label: Permanent working capital
points: Present in every month of the year, including the trough
Grows as the business grows, and never converts to cash
Behaves like a long-term asset even though it sits in current assets
Fund with own funds, retained profits, a term loan or a working capital term loan
Funding it with cash credit creates a permanent dependence on a facility repayable on demand

columns.label: Temporary working capital
points: Appears only in peak months and unwinds after the season
Driven by seasonality, festivals, a large one-off order or a price spike
Genuinely self-liquidating: the stock becomes invoices, which become cash
Fund with cash credit, overdraft, bill discounting or a seasonal peak limit
Funding it long-term leaves expensive money idle for much of the year

children.text: This is the
matching principle
, and its logic is simple. Money that has to be repaid or renewed before the asset turns into cash creates risk. Money that stays committed long after the asset has turned into cash creates waste.

markDefs.definition: Funding an asset with money whose tenor matches the life of that asset, so nothing has to be refinanced before it turns into cash.

body.caption: Three ways to fund the same year (₹ crore)

cells: Idle funds for eight months of the year
Balanced: ₹1.39 crore cheaper than funding it all long-term
Cheapest by ₹0.26 crore, but the permanent layer sits on a demand facility

children.text: Note how small the gap is between matched and fully short-term funding: ₹0.26 crore a year, about 26 lakh. That is the premium for sleeping at night. A business whose ₹17 crore permanent layer sits inside a cash credit limit is one annual review away from a crisis it cannot fix quickly.

body.label: A funding plan that matches the cycle
body.value: Own funds ₹10 crore, term loan ₹7 crore, cash credit limit ₹20 crore
body.context: The first two cover the permanent ₹17 crore and cannot be withdrawn. The cash credit limit of ₹20 crore covers the ₹19 crore seasonal peak with a small buffer, and sits largely unused in the quiet months.

children.text: How to Spot a Mismatch

You do not need the monthly chart to detect the problem. The cash credit account itself tells you. If the outstanding balance never falls below a certain level, that level is permanent working capital being funded by a demand facility.

body.title: Hardcore borrowing, and what banks do about it

children.text: Bankers call the never-repaid portion of a cash credit limit
hardcore borrowing

. A genuine working capital facility should swing: drawn during the build-up, repaid as collections arrive, with the account touching a credit balance at some point in the year. When it never swings, the facility is financing something permanent, and often something worse, such as a loss or a capital expenditure funded out of the limit.

markDefs.definition: The portion of a cash credit limit that is never repaid and simply stays drawn year round, revealing that a permanent need is being funded by a demand facility.

children.text: The usual remedy is to carve the hardcore portion out into a
working capital term loan

, which is repayable in instalments over three to five years, leaving a smaller cash credit limit that actually fluctuates. Borrowers often resist this, because a term loan forces real repayment while a limit can be rolled over indefinitely. That resistance is precisely the point: the repayment schedule surfaces the fact that the money was never temporary.

markDefs.definition: Working capital term loan. A repayable loan, often used to carve out the permanently drawn portion of a cash credit account and put it on a fixed repayment schedule.

children.text: Banks also sanction peak and non-peak limits for genuinely seasonal borrowers such as sugar mills, woollen units and agri processors. The borrower gets a higher limit for the defined peak months and a lower one for the rest of the year, and pays commitment charges accordingly. If your business is seasonal, ask for this structure rather than carrying one flat limit sized for the peak.

body.title: Read the cash credit account
body.question: A company has a ₹25 crore cash credit limit. Over the last three years, the outstanding balance has never fallen below ₹18 crore in any month. What does this tell you?
options: The company is using its limit efficiently and should ask for an increase
About ₹18 crore of permanent working capital is being funded by a facility repayable on demand
The bank has been charging too much interest on the limit
The company is clearly making losses
body.explanation: A cash credit limit is meant to fluctuate with the operating cycle. A floor of ₹18 crore that never clears means that much of the need is permanent, not seasonal. It may or may not signal losses, but it is definitely a tenor mismatch, and most banks will eventually ask for that portion to be converted into a repayable term loan.

children.text: There is a second reason the permanent layer deserves attention: it grows. If Himachal Knitwear grows 20% next year and its cycle stays the same, the permanent layer rises from ₹17 crore to about ₹20.4 crore. That extra ₹3.4 crore is not a seasonal bulge, it is new permanent funding the business has to arrange from long-term sources, every single year that it grows.

body.text: This is the quiet arithmetic behind most growth crises. Each year of growth adds a permanent layer that must be funded permanently. Profit alone often cannot cover it, which is why growing companies raise capital or take on term debt even when they are profitable.

body.title: Name the layer
body.textWithBlank: The portion of working capital that is present even in the quietest month of the year, and never converts back into cash while the business operates, is called ___ working capital.
body.explanation: Permanent working capital, also called core or fixed working capital, behaves like a long-term asset and should be funded with long-term money.

body.title: The bank wants to restructure the limit
body.scenario: A Ludhiana hosiery manufacturer has a ₹30 crore cash credit limit that has not fallen below ₹21 crore in four years. At the annual review, the bank proposes cutting the limit to ₹12 crore and converting ₹18 crore into a working capital term loan repayable over four years, at a rate 1.5 percentage points higher. The promoter is furious, saying the bank is punishing a customer who has never missed an interest payment.
body.prompt: Is the bank being unreasonable? What would you advise the promoter to do?
body.modelAnswer:
The bank is not being unreasonable. A limit that never falls below ₹21 crore is funding a permanent need with a facility repayable on demand. The bank is correcting a tenor mismatch that has been sitting on both balance sheets for four years.

What the promoter is really objecting to is repayment. Under the limit, the ₹21 crore never had to be paid back. Under a four-year term loan it does, at roughly ₹4.5 crore a year plus interest, and that has to come out of cash the business is currently using elsewhere. The higher rate is the smaller issue: on ₹18 crore, 1.5 percentage points is about ₹27 lakh a year.

What to advise. First, accept the principle but negotiate the terms: ask for a five-year tenor with a six-month moratorium, and for the cash credit limit to be set at a level that genuinely covers the seasonal swing rather than at ₹12 crore chosen arbitrarily. Second, produce the monthly working capital profile for the last two years, because that evidence, and not an argument, is what will size the limit correctly. Third, if the business is seasonal, ask for peak and non-peak limits instead of one flat number. Fourth, and most important, work out where the ₹21 crore actually went. If it funded machinery or losses rather than the operating cycle, the term loan is treating a symptom and the underlying problem needs its own answer.

body.title: Separate the two layers in your own business
steps: Pull the month-end working capital figure for each of the last 24 months, using inventory plus receivables minus payables.
Take the lowest month in each year: that is your permanent layer, and comparing the two years shows how fast it is growing.
Take the highest month: the difference from the lowest is the seasonal requirement your limit must cover.
Check the monthly minimum outstanding on your cash credit account over the same period to find the hardcore portion.
Compare the permanent layer with your long-term funding, that is own funds, retained profits and term loans.
If the permanent layer exceeds long-term funding, plan the correction before the bank raises it at the annual review.
Project next year's permanent layer by applying your planned growth rate, and arrange that funding in advance.

body.title: The vocabulary of the two layers

cards.definition: The minimum level present even in the quietest month. Grows with the business and never converts to cash.
The seasonal bulge above that minimum, which unwinds into cash after the peak.
Fund each layer with money whose tenor matches the life of the need: long-term for permanent, short-term for seasonal.
The portion of a cash credit limit that never gets repaid, showing a permanent need funded by a demand facility.
A repayable loan used to carve out hardcore borrowing and put it on a proper repayment schedule.
A sanctioned structure giving a seasonal borrower a higher limit during defined peak months and a lower one for the rest of the year.

body.text: Every rupee of growth adds a layer of working capital that never comes back. Seasonal needs unwind on their own. Permanent needs have to be funded permanently, and that is a decision, not an accident.

points: Working capital has two layers: a permanent level present even in the quietest month, and a temporary bulge that unwinds after the season.
The permanent layer behaves like a long-term asset and should be funded with own funds, retained profits or term debt.
The temporary layer is self-liquidating and belongs on cash credit, overdraft or bill discounting.
A single 31 March balance sheet can badly understate a seasonal business, so use monthly data to size both layers.
A cash credit balance that never falls to zero reveals hardcore borrowing, which banks typically convert into a working capital term loan.
Seasonal borrowers can ask for peak and non-peak limits rather than carrying one flat limit sized for the peak.
Growth adds to the permanent layer every year, and that funding has to be arranged in advance rather than discovered in a crisis.
